title: Counter melody as the signature on a tune
summary: Blumberg recalls Bunk's concept of a private counter theme embellished each time, and his revelation that jazz is formal, not wholly improvised.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The End whether he called it counter melody or counter theme or your chorus to play on it, he had some name for it, but he did mention that once, you know, that concept of having a counter melody for each tune, as if it's something that you're going to compose, you're going to be very caring about it, and use it all the time. And keep it in mind, and your own private property for that, just something you make up on this very moment. The signature, yeah, on the tune. And of course he would do this, but he would improvise on it each time, he'd play it a little different. Yeah, that's right. But I thought it was a very interesting concept of playing, you know, because it was one of the many revelations I had about jazz, which up until then I thought was 100% improvised, and that they played everything completely differently each time, you know, and then when I heard this band I realized that it's not that way at all. They play the same choruses and the same figures over and over again, but they embellish them differently and they use them differently. And it gives the music a kind of formalism that it wouldn't have, I think, if things were completely different each time.
Did Bunk ever mention to you about the dynamics of playing the starting out the first chorus loud or the hitting the introduction hard as they sometimes say here?
